## Methods

RNA sample preparation
Full-length Azoarcus pre-tRNAIle and L intron were individually cloned into the pUC19 vector. A T7 promoter sequence (5′-TAATACGACTCACTATA-3′) was appended to the 5′ end to enable in vitro transcription by T7 RNA polymerase. DNA templates were amplified via PCR using PrimeSTAR Max DNA Polymerase (TaKaRa), followed by ethanol precipitation and resuspension in DEPC-treated water. Purified DNA was stored at -20°C. In vitro transcription was performed in reactions containing 40 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.9), 5 mM MgCl₂, 2 mM spermidine, 0.01% Triton X-100, 5 mM DTT, 2 mM of each NTP, 0.2 U/μL recombinant RNase inhibitor (TaKaRa), 50 ng/μL linearized DNA template, and lab-purified T7 RNA polymerase. Reactions were incubated at 37°C for 4 hours. RNA transcripts were purified by denaturing urea–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (urea-PAGE). For pre-tRNAIle and L intron, transcripts were resolved on 6% urea-PAGE gels (acrylamide:bisacrylamide = 19:1) at 300 V for 4 hours. For C intron and C′ intron generated from L intron, transcripts were resolved on 15% urea-PAGE at 300 V for 72 hours. Gels were briefly visualized under UV light, and target bands were excised. RNA was eluted from gel slices in 300 mM sodium acetate (pH 5.2) containing 1 mM EDTA, rotating at 4°C for 12 hours. Eluates were concentrated using 30 kDa centrifugal filters (Millipore), mixed with an equal volume of isopropanol, and flash-frozen at -80°C for 10 minutes. Precipitated RNA was washed twice with 75% ethanol, air-dried, dissolved in DEPC-treated water, and stored at -80°C. Sequences of RNA constructs and related DNA primers are provided in Supplementary Data 1.

To generate the G37 point mutation, site-directed mutagenesis was performed using the ClonExpress® II One Step Cloning Kit (Vazyme), following the manufacturer’s protocol. Mutation-specific primers were designed accordingly, and PCR was carried out with PrimeSTAR Max DNA Polymerase (TaKaRa). The amplified product was treated with DpnI (New England Biolabs) to digest the methylated parental plasmid. The resulting product was ligated using the supplied recombination mix and transformed into competent E. coli cells. Mutant RNAs were transcribed and purified following the identical in vitro transcription and PAGE purification protocols established for the wild-type construct.

Cryo-EM sample preparation
Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) samples were prepared using an in vitro refolding strategy. RNA samples were first denatured by heating at 90°C for 3 min, then immediately diluted in refolding buffer to final concentrations of 40 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5) and 15 mM MgCl₂. The mixture was incubated at 37°C for 30 min to refold. For grid preparation, 4 μL of the RNA solution (20μM) was applied to glow-discharged 200-mesh R2/1 Quantifoil® copper grids. Grids were blotted once (blot force 0, blot time 4 s) after a 5-second wait time and rapidly cryocooled in rapid plunging into liquid ethane using a Vitrobot Mark IV (Thermo Fisher Scientific).

Cryo-EM data collection and processing
For pre-tRNAIle,L intron and C intron, the grids were imaged on a Titan Krios G3i cryo-EM microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at a magnification of 105,000x, corresponding to a calibrated pixel size of 0.82 Å. Micrographs were recorded by EPU software (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with a K3 camera. Each image consisted of 30 frames with an exposure time of 2.5 s and a total dose of 57.5-64 electrons per Å2. A total of 2,911 movie stacks for pre-tRNA, 2,888 movie stacks for the L intron, and 3,602 movie stacks for the C intron were collected, with a defocus range of -0.8 to -2.7 μm. For C′ intron, the grids were imaged on a Titan Krios G4 cryo-EM microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at a magnification of 130,000x, corresponding to a calibrated pixel size of 0.96 Å. Micrographs were recorded by EPU software (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with a Falcon4i camera. Each image consisted of 30 frames with an exposure time of 5.88 s and a total dose of 50 electrons per Å2. A total of 8,147 movie stacks for C′ intron were collected, with a defocus range of -0.8 to -1.5 μm. The details of data collection are summarized in Supplementary Table 1.

Data processing was performed using the software package cryoSPARC45. Micrographs were motion corrected with patch motion correction. The CTF parameters of micrographs were estimated using patch CTF estimation. All particles were autopicked using the template picker in cryoSPARC. After 2D classification, 100,0 00 random particles in good 2D classes were used for ab initio map generation followed by 3D heterogeneous refinement. The particles of the good 3D classes were then refined into higher resolution by non-uniform refinement. Resolution for the final map was estimated with the 0.143 criterion of the Fourier shell correlation curve. The resolution map was calculated in cryoSPARC using the “Local Resolution Estimation” option. The processing details are shown in Fig S1, 4, 5, 6 and listed in Supplementary Table 1.

Model building
The initial structural model of the full-length Azoarcus pre-tRNA was generated using AlphaFold346 and rigidly docked into the cryo-EM density of the pre-1S state. To achieve optimal fit, multiple iterations of molecular dynamics flexible fitting (MDFF)47 were performed until convergence. The resulting models were further corrected and refined using Coot48 and phenix.real_space_refine49. For the linear and circularized intron structures, the intron coordinates from the pre-1S model served as templates, which were similarly fitted into their respective cryo-EM maps, manually adjusted by Coot, and subsequently refined. The quality of the final atomic models was assessed using MolProbity50, with statistics provided in Supplementary Table 1. Structural figures were prepared using Chimera51 or ChimeraX52, and secondary structure schematics were generated with RiboDraw, followed by manual adjustments (https://github.com/ribokit/RiboDraw).

RNase R digestion assay
RNase R digestion was used to distinguish circular RNAs from linear species. Reactions (10 μL) were assembled on ice and contained 500 ng RNA, 1× RNase R reaction buffer, and 2 U RNase R (Beyotime). RNase R is a magnesium-dependent 3′→5′ exoribonuclease that selectively degrades linear RNAs while sparing circular forms. Samples were incubated at 37°C for 15 minutes, and the reaction was terminated by heating at 70°C for 10 minutes. An equal volume of 2× RNA loading buffer (95% formamide, 5 mM EDTA, 0.025% SDS, 0.02% xylene cyanol, 0.02% bromophenol blue) was added, followed by denaturation at 95°C for 5 minutes. Digestion products were resolved on an 8% denaturing urea–polyacrylamide gel (acrylamide:bis-acrylamide = 19:1) at 200 V for 3 hours. Gels were stained with 0.5× SuperRed nucleic acid stain (Biosharp) for 1 minute and visualized under 254-nm UV illumination using a gel documentation system (Peiqing Biotech).

Self-splicing Assays
Self-splicing reactions were performed through in vitro refolding followed by incubation at 37°C. For each reaction, 15 pmol pre-tRNAIle RNA were first denatured by heating at 90°C for 3 min. The samples were then immediately diluted in a refolding buffer to final concentrations of 40 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 15 mM MgCl₂, and 25 μM GTP. Separate reaction mixtures were then incubated at 37°C for 0, 5, 10, 30, 60, 120, and 180 min, respectively. At each designated time point, the corresponding reaction was quenched by adding an equal volume of 2× RNA loading buffer (95% formamide, 5 mM EDTA, 0.025% SDS, 0.02% xylene cyanol, and 0.02% bromophenol blue), followed by denaturation at 95°C for 5 min. Reaction products were resolved by 8% denaturing urea–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (acrylamide:bis-acrylamide = 19:1) under constant voltage (300 V) for 8 hours. Gels were stained for 1 min with 0.5× SuperRed nucleic acid stain (Biosharp) and visualized under 254-nm UV transillumination using a gel documentation system (Peiqing Biotech).

Circularization Assays
Two-step and second-step circularization reactions were performed through in vitro refolding followed by incubation at 37°C. For each reaction, 15 pmol of the appropriate RNA substrate (L intron for two-step circularization; C intron for second-step circularization) were first denatured by heating at 90°C for 3 min. The samples were then immediately diluted in a refolding buffer to final concentrations of 40 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5) and 15 mM MgCl₂. Separate reaction mixtures for two-step circularization were incubated at 37°C for 0, 10, 20, 30, 60, and 120 min, while those for second-step circularization were incubated for 0, 2, 4, and 6 h. At each designated time point, the corresponding reaction was quenched by adding an equal volume of 2× RNA loading buffer (95% formamide, 5 mM EDTA, 0.025% SDS, 0.02% xylene cyanol, and 0.02% bromophenol blue), followed by denaturation at 95°C for 5 min. Reaction products were resolved by 8% denaturing urea–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (acrylamide:bis-acrylamide = 19:1) under constant voltage (200 V) for 40 min. Gels were stained for 1 min with 0.5× SuperRed nucleic acid stain (Biosharp) and visualized under 254-nm UV transillumination using a gel documentation system (Peiqing Biotech).

Circularization of the L Intron with RNase Inhibitor
Circularization reactions of the L intron were performed in the presence or absence of RNase inhibitor. For each reaction, 12 pmol L intron were first denatured by heating at 90°C for 3 min. The samples were then immediately diluted in the refolding buffer to final concentrations of 40 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5) and 15 mM MgCl₂. Two parallel sets of reactions were set up: one group supplemented with 10% (v/v) TaKaRa Recombinant RNase Inhibitor (Cat. No. 2313A) (RRI, +), and the other group without RNase inhibitor (-). All reaction mixtures were then incubated at 37°C for 0-60 min. At designated time points (0, 30, and 60 min), equal aliquots were withdrawn and quenched by adding an equal volume of 2× RNA loading buffer (95% formamide, 5 mM EDTA, 0.025% SDS, 0.02% xylene cyanol, and 0.02% bromophenol blue), followed by denaturation at 95°C for 5 min. Reaction products were resolved by 8% denaturing urea–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (acrylamide:bis-acrylamide = 19:1) under constant voltage (200 V) for 3h. Gels were stained for 1 min with 0.5× SuperRed nucleic acid stain (Biosharp) and visualized under 254-nm UV transillumination using a gel documentation system (Peiqing Biotech).

Second-step Circularization of the C Intron under Different pH Conditions
Circularization reactions of the C intron were carried out under two different pH conditions (pH 7.5 and pH 6.0) to assess the effect of buffer acidity on the second-step ligation. For each reaction, 8 pmol C intron substrates were first denatured by heating at 90°C for 3 min, followed by immediate dilution into refolding buffers containing 15 mM MgCl₂ and either 40 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5) or 40 mM Tris-HCl (pH 6.0). All reaction mixtures were then incubated at 37°C for 0–6 h. At the designated time points (0, 3 h, and 6 h), equal aliquots were removed and quenched by addition of an equal volume of 2× RNA loading buffer (95% formamide, 5 mM EDTA, 0.025% SDS, 0.02% xylene cyanol, and 0.02% bromophenol blue), followed by denaturation at 95°C for 5 min. Reaction products were resolved by 8% denaturing urea–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (acrylamide:bis-acrylamide = 19:1) at a constant voltage of 200 V for 3 h. Gels were stained with 0.5× SuperRed nucleic acid stain (Biosharp) for 1 min and imaged under 254-nm UV transillumination using a gel documentation system (Peiqing Biotech).

Circularization Analysis Using Split L Intron Fragments
Circularization reactions were performed using split L intron fragments through in vitro refolding. For each reaction, 4 pmol of Fragment A (1-69 nt, containing two guanosine residues at the 5′ end and FAM-labeled) and 8 pmol of Fragment B (70-205 nt) were co-refolded. As a control, a separate reaction containing only 4 pmol of Fragment A without Fragment B was included. The RNA fragment mixtures were first denatured by heating at 90°C for 3 min. The samples were then immediately diluted in the refolding buffer to final concentrations of 40 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5) and 15 mM MgCl₂. The reaction mixtures were incubated at 37°C for 0, 2 and 4 h, while the control reaction (Fragment A only) was incubated for 2 h. All reactions were quenched by adding an equal volume of 2× RNA loading buffer (95% formamide, 5 mM EDTA, 0.025% SDS, 0.02% xylene cyanol, and 0.02% bromophenol blue), followed by denaturation at 95°C for 5 min. Reaction products were resolved using a 10%-20% gradient denaturing urea-polyacrylamide gel (acrylamide:bis-acrylamide = 19:1) under constant voltage (300 V) for 25 min. Following electrophoresis, gels were simultaneously subjected to two detection methods: GelRed staining (Biosharp) was used to detect longer RNA fragments using a gel documentation system (Peiqing Biotech), and FAM imaging was performed to detect short drop-off fragments using a Fast Laser Imager (Typhoon FLA 7000).

This manuscript describes an elegant investigation of a model self-splicing ribozyme isolated from Azoarcus pre-tRNA. The
authors use cryogenic to solve the structures of the pre-splicing conformation, which includes the intact, but unsliced pre-
tRNA visible in two stable conformations with respect to the ribozyme. This is the most important finding of the work–the fact
that in this system, as opposed to the twice-larger Tetrahymena ribozyme, the exons only base-pair with the internal guide
sequence, as predicted by phylogeny and biochemical studies, but never before visualized. Thus, this ribozyme is an ideal
catalytic RNA to be used for synthetic biology applications. In addition, this ribozyme folds via an apparent two-state
mechanism, avoiding complicated intermediates and misfolded states (perhaps the authors could point this out in the
discussion at the end of their manuscript where potential synth bio applications are mentioned). So in many ways, this the
simplest of the complicated ribozymes and now the authors show us why this is so from a structural biology perspective.
In addition, the authors provide two other states of the ribozyme post splicing – a major and a minor circularization product.
As expected, but here shown explicitly, the ribozyme does not undergo any major conformational changes, beyond
rearrangements in the P1 region where changes are needed for splicing and circularization. And a mechanism for the
selection of the circularization sites is presented, with three mutants supporting the model of a specific interaction.
Overall, this a well executed and written up study. I only have a few relatively minor
issues/suggestions:
1. The title could use a noun after “pre-splicing” such as “Pre-splicing conformation ..”
2. The gels and kinetics do not really support a sequential mechanism for C and C’ formation. Yes, if a specific state is
prepared (as in Fig 4b), C’ will be the new product, but that does not prove the sequential circularization. Instead, it looks
equally likely that C’ is simply a minor product resulting from a statistical distribution of the 5’ terminal sequences in the
active site. This ribozyme has no energy driving any of these reactions - they are all basically in equilibrium because they
are transesterifications, with the exception of the exogenous guanosine driving the first splicing reaction through chemical
potential. Everything else is reversible. The band intensities suggest (but the authors should do the measurements and
show the kinetics and provide the rate constants) that the rate at which C and C’ appear are similar, it’s just that the
amplitudes are vastly different. This issue should be resolved experimentally or through analysis of the existing kinetics.
3. Along point #2, it would help to resolve the small products - the 5’ cleaved sequences, for example by labeling the
ribozyme at the 5’ end and then running the kinetics to prove the relative kinetics and amplitudes of product formation.

## Paper

## Abstract

Group I introns are catalytic RNAs capable of self-splicing, yet structural insights into full-length precursor RNAs and post-splicing circularization have been limited. Here, we present cryo-EM structures of the Azoarcus pre-tRNAIle system across key catalytic stages, including the full-length precursor in Pre-1S conformations, the linear intron, and the circular introns, at 2.8-3.3 Å resolution. These structures reveal a preformed P1 helix, register shifts during splicing, and a conformational flip of G37 that stabilizes the circularization site. Biochemical analyses confirm a two-step circularization mechanism, generating a secondary circular product via an alternative ligation site. Together, our results provide the atomic-level view of a group I intron system through splicing and circularization. This work uncovers structural principles governing RNA conformational dynamics, catalysis, and circular RNA formation, with broad implications for ribozyme engineering.

---

## Introduction

Group I introns are a class of catalytic RNAs capable of self-splicing through two consecutive transesterification reactions, excising themselves from precursor RNAs and ligating the flanking exons1,2. This process is facilitated by a conserved catalytic core and complex tertiary interactions, often modulated by divalent metal ions and exogenous guanosine3–5. Owing to their robust catalytic capacity and ancient evolutionary origin, group I introns have served as valuable models for understanding RNA structure, catalysis, and the evolution of ribozymes6–12.

While extensive structural studies, particularly on the Tetrahymena thermophila and Azoarcus group I introns, have provided snapshots of ribozymes in splicing-relevant conformations, most available data are limited to constructs with truncated exons or inactive precursors13–18. As a result, the structural basis underlying pre-tRNA folding and the post-splicing fate of the intron, particularly circularization, remains poorly defined. Circular forms of Group I introns have been observed in various systems, where the terminal guanosine initiates an internal nucleophilic attack to produce 5′-truncated circular RNAs19–22. These circular RNAs are thought to regulate RNA turnover, avoid harmful reverse splicing, or serve as templates for homing endonucleases23,24.

The Group I intron from Azoarcus sp. BH72 pre-tRNAIle is a model system with robust self-splicing and circularization abilities25–27. It s compact 205-nt intron resides in the anticodon loop region of the tRNA, and lacks several peripheral domains found in Tetrahymena introns8. Previous crystal structures have captured a catalytically primed state of the Azoarcus ribozyme with short exons, yet failed to represent the full precursor architecture or subsequent conformational transitions following exon ligation15–17.

Here, we employ cryo-EM to resolve high-resolution structures of three key intermediates in the Azoarcus group I intron splicing pathway: the full-length precursor at the Pre-1S state, the linear intron, and the circular introns. Together with biochemical validation, these structures reveal a two-step circularization mechanism in which the P1ext helix undergoes a defined 2-nucleotide register shift after exon ligation, repositioning the catalytic core for intron circularization. This work provides the unprecedented near atomic-resolution view of a complete Azoarcus group I intron splicing and circularization trajectory, offering new mechanistic insights into RNA conformational plasticity, catalysis, and post-splicing processing.

---

## Results

Cryo-EM revealed the Full-Length Azoarcus Pre-tRNAIle at Pre-1S states
Previous crystallographic studies of the Azoarcus group I intron have provided important insights into ribozyme catalysis, especially at stages mimicking the second step of self-splicing16,17. However, these structures typically relied on constructs containing truncated exons and lacked visualization of the full-length pre-tRNA substrate, particularly its structural organization before the first transesterification event. Moreover, the post-splicing fate of the intron, namely its circularization, remained structurally uncharacterized. To bridge this knowledge gap, we investigated the full-length Azoarcus Pre-tRNAIle (284 nt), which contains a catalytic group I intron (205 nt) located in the anticodon loop region of the tRNA, aiming to capture both the pre-splicing and post-splicing states (Fig. 1a-b). Using in vitro splicing assays at physiological temperature (37°C)26,28, we confirmed that this RNA undergoes efficient self-splicing, generating three major products over time: mature tRNA, linear intron (L intron), and circular intron (C intron), with a corresponding reduction in precursor RNA abundance (Fig. 1c). These results verified the system’s robust ability to perform both exon ligation and intron circularization, highlighting its suitability for structural investigation.

We initially conducted single-particle cryo-EM analysis of full-length pre-tRNA following incubation at 37°C for 30 minutes to capture structural intermediates during self-splicing. However, likely due to the conformational heterogeneity of the sample, the resulting maps lacked sufficient resolution for reliable model building. To overcome this limitation, we prepared three distinct RNA samples representing key stages in the splicing pathway: (1) the pre-splicing state using full-length pre-tRNA without added GTP (Fig. S1a); ( 2) the linear intron after splicing; and (3) the circular intron after post-splicing circularization. Cryo-EM analysis of the pre-tRNA sample yielded two distinct conformational states at 3.11 Å and 3.06 Å resolutions, respectively, representing early pre-catalytic intermediates (Pre-1S) (Fig. 1d, Fig. S1b-g, Supplementary Table 1, and Supplementary Movie 1). In both structures, the 5′ exon has already aligned with the internal guide sequence (IGS) to form the canonical P1 helix, while the 3′ exon remains unpaired, positioning the molecule for the first transesterification reaction. Notably, even though no exogenous G was added during sample preparation, weak density corresponding to guanosine was observed in the G-binding pocket, possibly originating from RNA degradation (Fig. 1d-e, Fig. S2a). Comparative analysis of the two Pre-1S states revealed notable conformational flexibility in the tRNA anticodon domain, characterized by an approximately 45° rotational difference between Pre-1S_a and Pre-1S_b (Fig. S2b-d, S3a). This motion likely reflects intrinsic flexibility at the intron–tRNA junction, which contains a single-stranded region (Fig. 1d). These two states likely represent distinct local minima on the RNA’s energy landscape, reflecting dynamic sampling of catalytically permissive conformations prior to exon ligation.

Besides the tRNA exons, both the Pre-1S structures consist of the canonical RNA elements of group I intron (P2, P3, P4, P5, P6, P7, P8, P9, and P9.0) and adopts the canonical architecture seen in previously reported Azoarcus ribozyme structures16,29(Fig. S3b-c). This conservation underscores the structural stability of the catalytic domain even in the context of full-length tRNA exons and emphasizes the conservation of the group I intron fold. Together, our structures provide a high-resolution view of a full-length pre-tRNA substrate poised near the onset of catalysis, offering insight into early structural events associated with tRNA maturation and intron excision.

2-nt sliding of P1 helix between Linear Intron and Pre-tRNA
To investigate the structural transitions underpinning post-splicing and circularization of the Azoarcus group I intron, we determined high-resolution cryo-EM structures of the excised linear intron (L intron; Post-2S) and the subsequent circular introns (C and C′ introns; Post-C) at 3.01 Å resolution for L, 3.27 Å and 2.86 Å resolutions for C and C′ introns (Figs. 2-5, Figs. S4-6, Supplementary Table 1, and Supplementary Movie 1). These reconstructions allowed us to examine in detail how the intron architecture evolves following exon ligation and prepares for circularization.

Structural comparison between the Pre-1S and L intron states revealed that while the global scaffold of the ribozyme, including peripheral domains and the G-binding pocket, remained largely conserved, the P1/P1ext region underwent a notable conformational shift (Fig. 2b-e, Fig. S3d-e). In the Pre-1S state, the P1/P1ext helix is formed via base pairing between the 5′ exon and the internal guide sequence (IGS), aligning the 5′ splice site for nucleophilic attack. Following exon ligation and tRNA release, the P1ext helix is reformed within the intron alone, through intramolecular pairing between the free 5′ end and IGS. Importantly, the newly formed P1ext helix in the linear intron undergoes a 2-nt register shift relative to its position in the Pre-1S state, bringing the circularization reaction nucleophile, the 3′-OH of G205 (ωG, the 3′ terminal G) into planar alignment with the phosphodiester bond between U2 and U3, thus positioning the molecule in a circularization-ready conformation (Fig. 2f).

This finding highlights a key mechanism by which the ribozyme repurposes the same structural framework to carry out two distinct catalytic reactions: exon ligation and subsequent intron circularization. The observed register shift in the P1ext helix underscores the dynamic adaptability of group I introns, allowing them to reconfigure their base-pairing interactions to execute multiple reaction steps with high precision. In addition, we noticed that the density near the G-1 position in the L intron closely resembles the “pseudo-triple-helix” configuration recently described in another group I intron30. This region shows a continuous strand folding back onto the P1ext helix through non-canonical hydrogen bonds and stacking interactions, forming a pseudo-triple-helix–like tertiary contact (Fig. S4g). This interaction likely helps stabilize P1ext during circularization.

G37 reorientation anchors the circularization site and enhances efficiency
High-resolution cryo-EM structures of the L intron and the C intron revealed striking conservation across most of the ribozyme scaffold, particularly within the P1ext helix, which remains compact and nearly identical between the two states (Fig. 3a-b, Fig. S3f, S4, S5, S7, and Supplementary Movie 1). Despite this structural similarity, a single pronounced conformational change was observed during circularization: nucleotide G37 undergoes a distinct reorientation, flipping inward from its original outward-facing configuration while forming a Hoogsteen pair with G11 (Fig. 3c).

To assess the functional significance of G37, we performed site-directed mutagenesis to substitute this residue with A, C, or U, followed by in vitro circularization assays. Among the variants, the G37C mutant displayed a markedly increased yield of circular intron relative to the wild type (Fig. 3d), suggesting enhanced stabilization of the circularization site. This is likely due to the increased thermodynamic stability of the C37-G11 base pair compared to the original G-G pairing. In contrast, the G37A and G37U substitutions failed to promote circularization, indicating that the base-pairing potential and positioning of G37 are critical for productive catalysis. Together, these results identify G37 as a key conformational determinant in the circularization pathway of group I introns. Its dynamic reorientation not only marks a structural transition point but also fine-tunes the local architecture to optimize catalytic efficiency. This underscores a broader principle wherein single-nucleotide conformational switches can exert outsized influence on RNA processing outcomes by stabilizing transient but functionally important RNA configurations.

Identification and Validation of a Secondary Circularization Product
During prolonged incubation of Azoarcus pre-tRNA at 37°C, we observed the emergence of a lower-migrating RNA band beneath the canonical C intron, most clearly visible after 180 minutes (Fig. 1c). This unexpected product, designated as the C′ intron, suggested the possibility of an additional circular RNA species arising through a secondary processing event. The appearance of this smaller circular RNA recalls similar two-step circularization mechanisms reported in Tetrahymena group I introns31–34, prompting us to explore whether the Azoarcus system follows a comparable pathway. To investigate the origin of C′ intron, we conducted in vitro circularization assays using linear intron RNA. Gel electrophoresis revealed the presence of three distinct products: the C intron, the L-3 intron, and the C′ intron. This observation suggests that the C intron may undergo ring opening to form the L-3 linear intron33,34, which subsequently undergoes a second circularization event to generate the C′ intron, thereby supporting a model of sequential processing (Fig. 4a).

To validate the circular nature of both C and C′ introns, we treated the products with RNase R, a 3′-5′ exonuclease that selectively degrades linear RNAs while sparing circular forms. As expected, RNase R treatment led to complete degradation of the linear intron, while the C and C′ introns remained intact (Fig. 4b), confirming their circular topology35. We then employed reverse transcription followed by high-throughput sequencing to precisely map the ligation junctions of both products. Sequencing results revealed that the C intron is circularized at the L-3 position, resulting in the loss of the 5′-terminal GAU trinucleotide (Fig. 4c), whereas the C′ intron is circularized at the L-5 position, involving the removal of a GAUUU pentanucleotide (Fig. 4d). To test whether C′ intron formation occurs via a ring-opened intermediate, we purified C intron and incubated it under standard circularization conditions. Time-course experiments showed efficient conversion of C to C′ (Fig. 4e), confirming that C′ formation proceeds through secondary circularization following C intron opening33,34. Supporting this, 5′-FAM labeling detected only a 4-nt GGAU fragment corresponding to C intron formation, with no 6-nt GGAUUU fragment indicative of a direct conversion from L intron to C′ intron (Fig. 4f). Furthermore, inclusion of a recombinant RNase inhibitor to suppress potential enzymatic cleavage did not prevent the formation of the C′ intron (Fig. S8a). To further assess whether this conversion reflects a water driven, non-enzymatic process, we compared reactions performed under the original condition (pH 7.5) with those carried out under acidic conditions (pH 6.0). Under the neutral condition, hydrolysis of the C intron produced the linear L 3 intron and a clear C′ intron band was detected. In contrast, under acidic conditions, no detectable C′ intron was observed (Fig. S8b). Together, these observations support the interpretation that C′ intron formation is consistent with a water driven, non-enzymatic reaction that is intrinsic to the catalytic RNA.

To gain structural insight into the second circularization product, we determined the cryo-EM structure of the C′ intron at 2.86 Å resolution (Fig. 5a). The overall fold of the ribozyme remains largely conserved relative to the canonical C intron, however, pronounced structural remodeling occurs in the P1ext region (Fig. S3g). In contrast to the compact and fully base-paired P1ext observed in the C intron, the C′ intron displays extensive local unwinding, where nearly all base pairs in this region are disrupted except for the G11-G37 interaction, leaving the segment predominantly single-stranded (Fig. 5b-c and Fig. S7c). This partial melting appears to expand the solvent-exposed cavity adjacent to the catalytic center and may increase local flexibility near the ωG. The observed relaxation of P1ext is consistent with the biochemical evidence for a second, water-driven transesterification step, suggesting that such unwinding could facilitate repositioning of the phosphodiester bond between ωG and C5 for the subsequent ligation event. Together, these results reveal that the Azoarcus group I intron undergoes a two-step circularization process, highlighting a sequential and dynamic pathway reminiscent of Tetrahymena introns33,34.

Coordination of Catalytic Metal Ions Across Splicing and Circularization States
Metal ions play essential roles in group I intron catalysis, where five specific ions (M -M ) have been proposed to form the essential catalytic center. Through cryo-EM analysis of five functional states, including Pre-1S_a, Pre-1S_b, the L intron, the C intron, and the C′ intron, we identified and characterized three metal ion sites, designated M ,M and M (Fig. S9). The M ion displays state-dependent coordination geometry. In Pre-1S conformations, M associates with non-bridging phosphate oxygens of C87, G169, and A171 within the intron core. In the same states, M is positioned near the catalytic center and coordinates the nonbridging phosphate oxygens of G127 and A171, together with the 2′ and 3′ hydroxyl groups of ExoG. This coordination geometry suggests that M may contribute to stabilizing the leaving group and may act in concert with M to support a catalytically competent configuration. During the first circularization step, the key nucleotide U3 at the circularization site undergoes a conformational rearrangement that places its phosphate group within the coordination sphere of both M and M . This rearrangement likely anchors the circularization site within the catalytic core. Concurrently, M coordinates with the 2′ and 3′ hydroxyl groups of ωG, which may facilitate proper positioning of ωG during catalysis. The M ion lies peripherally to the active site and maintains stable coordination with the non-bridging phosphate oxygens of U172 and A173 in all observed states. This conserved geometry likely stabilizes the tertiary architecture of the P9.0 domain and contributes to maintaining the integrity of the ribozyme’s scaffold.

Beyond these established metal sites, we identified an additional ion in the catalytic core occupying the M position previously reported in Tetrahymena ribozymes14. This M coordinates the non-bridging phosphate oxygen of A86 and the 3′-OH of G127. The conservation of this position among group I introns suggests a possible catalytic or structural role, although its precise function remains to be determined. Together, these findings reveal that while the metallo-active core maintains a conserved overall architecture, the coordination geometries of individual ions adjust dynamically in response to transitions between splicing and circularization. This structural plasticity provides a mechanistic basis for how group I introns accommodate distinct chemical reactions while preserving catalytic precision.

Proposed Two-Step Circularization Mechanism
Integrating our structural and biochemical findings, along with previously established models such as the Tetrahymena IVS RNA circularization pathway31–34, we propose a two-step circularization mechanism for the Azoarcus pre-tRNA intron that operates through a “conformational rearrangement-sequential cleavage” framework (Fig. 5d). Following canonical self-splicing, the excised linear intron adopts a catalytically competent conformation through structural reorganization of the P1ext helix. This rearrangement aligns the phosphodiester bond between U2 and U3 within the ribozyme active site. The 3′-hydroxyl group of the conserved catalytic residue ωG then initiates a site-specific intramolecular transesterification reaction at U2, resulting in cleavage at the L-3 site and release of a 3-nt 5′ fragment (GAU). This first ligation event yields the primary circular species, termed the C intron. Subsequently, under near-neutral pH, the C intron undergoes spontaneous hydrolysis at the ligated junction, generating an L-3 linear intermediate33,34. This event promotes register shift of the P1ext helix, which in turn exposes a second phosphodiester bond between U4 and C5. A second transesterification reaction is then catalyzed by ωG, leading to cleavage at the L-5 site and release of a UU dinucleotide, ultimately forming the second circular product, C′ intron.

While this sequential pathway is supported by biochemical data, we cannot exclude the possibility of an alternative route. Specifically, a subset of linear introns may adopt a flexible P1ext conformation de novo, enabling ωG to bypass the L-3 reaction and directly cleave at the U4-C5 site32. This single-step mechanism would yield the C′ intron via release of a 5-nt fragment (GAUUU), reflecting a shortcut within the broader circularization pathway (Fig. 5d). However, as described above, our 5′-FAM labeling experiments detected no 6-nt GGAUUU product under standard in vitro conditions, confirming that direct conversion from the L intron to the C′ intron does not occur in our reconstituted system. While we cannot exclude the possibility that cellular factors or specific physiological conditions might enable this alternative route in vivo, our results indicate that the C intron-mediated sequential pathway represents the predominant mechanism of C′ intron formation under the tested conditions. Together, these results reveal a mechanistically versatile circularization program within group I introns, governed by dynamic P1ext remodeling and catalyzed through the strategic positioning of reactive residues and substrates. This work not only expands our understanding of intron self-processing but also provides a conceptual framework for engineering programmable RNA circularization systems.

## Methods

RNA sample preparation
Full-length Azoarcus pre-tRNAIle and L intron were individually cloned into the pUC19 vector. A T7 promoter sequence (5′-TAATACGACTCACTATA-3′) was appended to the 5′ end to enable in vitro transcription by T7 RNA polymerase. DNA templates were amplified via PCR using PrimeSTAR Max DNA Polymerase (TaKaRa), followed by ethanol precipitation and resuspension in DEPC-treated water. Purified DNA was stored at -20°C. In vitro transcription was performed in reactions containing 40 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.9), 5 mM MgCl₂, 2 mM spermidine, 0.01% Triton X-100, 5 mM DTT, 2 mM of each NTP, 0.2 U/μL recombinant RNase inhibitor (TaKaRa), 50 ng/μL linearized DNA template, and lab-purified T7 RNA polymerase. Reactions were incubated at 37°C for 4 hours. RNA transcripts were purified by denaturing urea–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (urea-PAGE). For pre-tRNAIle and L intron, transcripts were resolved on 6% urea-PAGE gels (acrylamide:bisacrylamide = 19:1) at 300 V for 4 hours. For C intron and C′ intron generated from L intron, transcripts were resolved on 15% urea-PAGE at 300 V for 72 hours. Gels were briefly visualized under UV light, and target bands were excised. RNA was eluted from gel slices in 300 mM sodium acetate (pH 5.2) containing 1 mM EDTA, rotating at 4°C for 12 hours. Eluates were concentrated using 30 kDa centrifugal filters (Millipore), mixed with an equal volume of isopropanol, and flash-frozen at -80°C for 10 minutes. Precipitated RNA was washed twice with 75% ethanol, air-dried, dissolved in DEPC-treated water, and stored at -80°C. Sequences of RNA constructs and related DNA primers are provided in Supplementary Data 1.

To generate the G37 point mutation, site-directed mutagenesis was performed using the ClonExpress® II One Step Cloning Kit (Vazyme), following the manufacturer’s protocol. Mutation-specific primers were designed accordingly, and PCR was carried out with PrimeSTAR Max DNA Polymerase (TaKaRa). The amplified product was treated with DpnI (New England Biolabs) to digest the methylated parental plasmid. The resulting product was ligated using the supplied recombination mix and transformed into competent E. coli cells. Mutant RNAs were transcribed and purified following the identical in vitro transcription and PAGE purification protocols established for the wild-type construct.

Cryo-EM sample preparation
Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) samples were prepared using an in vitro refolding strategy. RNA samples were first denatured by heating at 90°C for 3 min, then immediately diluted in refolding buffer to final concentrations of 40 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5) and 15 mM MgCl₂. The mixture was incubated at 37°C for 30 min to refold. For grid preparation, 4 μL of the RNA solution (20μM) was applied to glow-discharged 200-mesh R2/1 Quantifoil® copper grids. Grids were blotted once (blot force 0, blot time 4 s) after a 5-second wait time and rapidly cryocooled in rapid plunging into liquid ethane using a Vitrobot Mark IV (Thermo Fisher Scientific).

Cryo-EM data collection and processing
For pre-tRNAIle,L intron and C intron, the grids were imaged on a Titan Krios G3i cryo-EM microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at a magnification of 105,000x, corresponding to a calibrated pixel size of 0.82 Å. Micrographs were recorded by EPU software (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with a K3 camera. Each image consisted of 30 frames with an exposure time of 2.5 s and a total dose of 57.5-64 electrons per Å2. A total of 2,911 movie stacks for pre-tRNA, 2,888 movie stacks for the L intron, and 3,602 movie stacks for the C intron were collected, with a defocus range of -0.8 to -2.7 μm. For C′ intron, the grids were imaged on a Titan Krios G4 cryo-EM microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at a magnification of 130,000x, corresponding to a calibrated pixel size of 0.96 Å. Micrographs were recorded by EPU software (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with a Falcon4i camera. Each image consisted of 30 frames with an exposure time of 5.88 s and a total dose of 50 electrons per Å2. A total of 8,147 movie stacks for C′ intron were collected, with a defocus range of -0.8 to -1.5 μm. The details of data collection are summarized in Supplementary Table 1.

Data processing was performed using the software package cryoSPARC45. Micrographs were motion corrected with patch motion correction. The CTF parameters of micrographs were estimated using patch CTF estimation. All particles were autopicked using the template picker in cryoSPARC. After 2D classification, 100,0 00 random particles in good 2D classes were used for ab initio map generation followed by 3D heterogeneous refinement. The particles of the good 3D classes were then refined into higher resolution by non-uniform refinement. Resolution for the final map was estimated with the 0.143 criterion of the Fourier shell correlation curve. The resolution map was calculated in cryoSPARC using the “Local Resolution Estimation” option. The processing details are shown in Fig S1, 4, 5, 6 and listed in Supplementary Table 1.

Model building
The initial structural model of the full-length Azoarcus pre-tRNA was generated using AlphaFold346 and rigidly docked into the cryo-EM density of the pre-1S state. To achieve optimal fit, multiple iterations of molecular dynamics flexible fitting (MDFF)47 were performed until convergence. The resulting models were further corrected and refined using Coot48 and phenix.real_space_refine49. For the linear and circularized intron structures, the intron coordinates from the pre-1S model served as templates, which were similarly fitted into their respective cryo-EM maps, manually adjusted by Coot, and subsequently refined. The quality of the final atomic models was assessed using MolProbity50, with statistics provided in Supplementary Table 1. Structural figures were prepared using Chimera51 or ChimeraX52, and secondary structure schematics were generated with RiboDraw, followed by manual adjustments (https://github.com/ribokit/RiboDraw).

RNase R digestion assay
RNase R digestion was used to distinguish circular RNAs from linear species. Reactions (10 μL) were assembled on ice and contained 500 ng RNA, 1× RNase R reaction buffer, and 2 U RNase R (Beyotime). RNase R is a magnesium-dependent 3′→5′ exoribonuclease that selectively degrades linear RNAs while sparing circular forms. Samples were incubated at 37°C for 15 minutes, and the reaction was terminated by heating at 70°C for 10 minutes. An equal volume of 2× RNA loading buffer (95% formamide, 5 mM EDTA, 0.025% SDS, 0.02% xylene cyanol, 0.02% bromophenol blue) was added, followed by denaturation at 95°C for 5 minutes. Digestion products were resolved on an 8% denaturing urea–polyacrylamide gel (acrylamide:bis-acrylamide = 19:1) at 200 V for 3 hours. Gels were stained with 0.5× SuperRed nucleic acid stain (Biosharp) for 1 minute and visualized under 254-nm UV illumination using a gel documentation system (Peiqing Biotech).

Self-splicing Assays
Self-splicing reactions were performed through in vitro refolding followed by incubation at 37°C. For each reaction, 15 pmol pre-tRNAIle RNA were first denatured by heating at 90°C for 3 min. The samples were then immediately diluted in a refolding buffer to final concentrations of 40 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 15 mM MgCl₂, and 25 μM GTP. Separate reaction mixtures were then incubated at 37°C for 0, 5, 10, 30, 60, 120, and 180 min, respectively. At each designated time point, the corresponding reaction was quenched by adding an equal volume of 2× RNA loading buffer (95% formamide, 5 mM EDTA, 0.025% SDS, 0.02% xylene cyanol, and 0.02% bromophenol blue), followed by denaturation at 95°C for 5 min. Reaction products were resolved by 8% denaturing urea–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (acrylamide:bis-acrylamide = 19:1) under constant voltage (300 V) for 8 hours. Gels were stained for 1 min with 0.5× SuperRed nucleic acid stain (Biosharp) and visualized under 254-nm UV transillumination using a gel documentation system (Peiqing Biotech).

Circularization Assays
Two-step and second-step circularization reactions were performed through in vitro refolding followed by incubation at 37°C. For each reaction, 15 pmol of the appropriate RNA substrate (L intron for two-step circularization; C intron for second-step circularization) were first denatured by heating at 90°C for 3 min. The samples were then immediately diluted in a refolding buffer to final concentrations of 40 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5) and 15 mM MgCl₂. Separate reaction mixtures for two-step circularization were incubated at 37°C for 0, 10, 20, 30, 60, and 120 min, while those for second-step circularization were incubated for 0, 2, 4, and 6 h. At each designated time point, the corresponding reaction was quenched by adding an equal volume of 2× RNA loading buffer (95% formamide, 5 mM EDTA, 0.025% SDS, 0.02% xylene cyanol, and 0.02% bromophenol blue), followed by denaturation at 95°C for 5 min. Reaction products were resolved by 8% denaturing urea–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (acrylamide:bis-acrylamide = 19:1) under constant voltage (200 V) for 40 min. Gels were stained for 1 min with 0.5× SuperRed nucleic acid stain (Biosharp) and visualized under 254-nm UV transillumination using a gel documentation system (Peiqing Biotech).

Circularization of the L Intron with RNase Inhibitor
Circularization reactions of the L intron were performed in the presence or absence of RNase inhibitor. For each reaction, 12 pmol L intron were first denatured by heating at 90°C for 3 min. The samples were then immediately diluted in the refolding buffer to final concentrations of 40 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5) and 15 mM MgCl₂. Two parallel sets of reactions were set up: one group supplemented with 10% (v/v) TaKaRa Recombinant RNase Inhibitor (Cat. No. 2313A) (RRI, +), and the other group without RNase inhibitor (-). All reaction mixtures were then incubated at 37°C for 0-60 min. At designated time points (0, 30, and 60 min), equal aliquots were withdrawn and quenched by adding an equal volume of 2× RNA loading buffer (95% formamide, 5 mM EDTA, 0.025% SDS, 0.02% xylene cyanol, and 0.02% bromophenol blue), followed by denaturation at 95°C for 5 min. Reaction products were resolved by 8% denaturing urea–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (acrylamide:bis-acrylamide = 19:1) under constant voltage (200 V) for 3h. Gels were stained for 1 min with 0.5× SuperRed nucleic acid stain (Biosharp) and visualized under 254-nm UV transillumination using a gel documentation system (Peiqing Biotech).

Second-step Circularization of the C Intron under Different pH Conditions
Circularization reactions of the C intron were carried out under two different pH conditions (pH 7.5 and pH 6.0) to assess the effect of buffer acidity on the second-step ligation. For each reaction, 8 pmol C intron substrates were first denatured by heating at 90°C for 3 min, followed by immediate dilution into refolding buffers containing 15 mM MgCl₂ and either 40 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5) or 40 mM Tris-HCl (pH 6.0). ## Paper

## Abstract

Group I introns are catalytic RNAs capable of self-splicing, yet structural insights into full-length precursor RNAs and post-splicing circularization have been limited. Here, we present cryo-EM structures of the Azoarcus pre-tRNAIle system across key catalytic stages, including the full-length precursor in Pre-1S conformations, the linear intron, and the circular introns, at 2.8-3.3 Å resolution. These structures reveal a preformed P1 helix, register shifts during splicing, and a conformational flip of G37 that stabilizes the circularization site. Biochemical analyses confirm a two-step circularization mechanism, generating a secondary circular product via an alternative ligation site. Together, our results provide the atomic-level view of a group I intron system through splicing and circularization. This work uncovers structural principles governing RNA conformational dynamics, catalysis, and circular RNA formation, with broad implications for ribozyme engineering.

---

## Introduction

Group I introns are a class of catalytic RNAs capable of self-splicing through two consecutive transesterification reactions, excising themselves from precursor RNAs and ligating the flanking exons1,2. This process is facilitated by a conserved catalytic core and complex tertiary interactions, often modulated by divalent metal ions and exogenous guanosine3–5. Owing to their robust catalytic capacity and ancient evolutionary origin, group I introns have served as valuable models for understanding RNA structure, catalysis, and the evolution of ribozymes6–12.

While extensive structural studies, particularly on the Tetrahymena thermophila and Azoarcus group I introns, have provided snapshots of ribozymes in splicing-relevant conformations, most available data are limited to constructs with truncated exons or inactive precursors13–18. As a result, the structural basis underlying pre-tRNA folding and the post-splicing fate of the intron, particularly circularization, remains poorly defined. Circular forms of Group I introns have been observed in various systems, where the terminal guanosine initiates an internal nucleophilic attack to produce 5′-truncated circular RNAs19–22. These circular RNAs are thought to regulate RNA turnover, avoid harmful reverse splicing, or serve as templates for homing endonucleases23,24.

The Group I intron from Azoarcus sp. BH72 pre-tRNAIle is a model system with robust self-splicing and circularization abilities25–27. It s compact 205-nt intron resides in the anticodon loop region of the tRNA, and lacks several peripheral domains found in Tetrahymena introns8. Previous crystal structures have captured a catalytically primed state of the Azoarcus ribozyme with short exons, yet failed to represent the full precursor architecture or subsequent conformational transitions following exon ligation15–17.

Here, we employ cryo-EM to resolve high-resolution structures of three key intermediates in the Azoarcus group I intron splicing pathway: the full-length precursor at the Pre-1S state, the linear intron, and the circular introns. Together with biochemical validation, these structures reveal a two-step circularization mechanism in which the P1ext helix undergoes a defined 2-nucleotide register shift after exon ligation, repositioning the catalytic core for intron circularization. This work provides the unprecedented near atomic-resolution view of a complete Azoarcus group I intron splicing and circularization trajectory, offering new mechanistic insights into RNA conformational plasticity, catalysis, and post-splicing processing.

---

## Results

Cryo-EM revealed the Full-Length Azoarcus Pre-tRNAIle at Pre-1S states
Previous crystallographic studies of the Azoarcus group I intron have provided important insights into ribozyme catalysis, especially at stages mimicking the second step of self-splicing16,17. However, these structures typically relied on constructs containing truncated exons and lacked visualization of the full-length pre-tRNA substrate, particularly its structural organization before the first transesterification event. Moreover, the post-splicing fate of the intron, namely its circularization, remained structurally uncharacterized. To bridge this knowledge gap, we investigated the full-length Azoarcus Pre-tRNAIle (284 nt), which contains a catalytic group I intron (205 nt) located in the anticodon loop region of the tRNA, aiming to capture both the pre-splicing and post-splicing states (Fig. 1a-b). Using in vitro splicing assays at physiological temperature (37°C)26,28, we confirmed that this RNA undergoes efficient self-splicing, generating three major products over time: mature tRNA, linear intron (L intron), and circular intron (C intron), with a corresponding reduction in precursor RNA abundance (Fig. 1c). These results verified the system’s robust ability to perform both exon ligation and intron circularization, highlighting its suitability for structural investigation.

We initially conducted single-particle cryo-EM analysis of full-length pre-tRNA following incubation at 37°C for 30 minutes to capture structural intermediates during self-splicing. However, likely due to the conformational heterogeneity of the sample, the resulting maps lacked sufficient resolution for reliable model building. To overcome this limitation, we prepared three distinct RNA samples representing key stages in the splicing pathway: (1) the pre-splicing state using full-length pre-tRNA without added GTP (Fig. S1a); ( 2) the linear intron after splicing; and (3) the circular intron after post-splicing circularization. Cryo-EM analysis of the pre-tRNA sample yielded two distinct conformational states at 3.11 Å and 3.06 Å resolutions, respectively, representing early pre-catalytic intermediates (Pre-1S) (Fig. 1d, Fig. S1b-g, Supplementary Table 1, and Supplementary Movie 1). In both structures, the 5′ exon has already aligned with the internal guide sequence (IGS) to form the canonical P1 helix, while the 3′ exon remains unpaired, positioning the molecule for the first transesterification reaction. Notably, even though no exogenous G was added during sample preparation, weak density corresponding to guanosine was observed in the G-binding pocket, possibly originating from RNA degradation (Fig. 1d-e, Fig. S2a). Comparative analysis of the two Pre-1S states revealed notable conformational flexibility in the tRNA anticodon domain, characterized by an approximately 45° rotational difference between Pre-1S_a and Pre-1S_b (Fig. S2b-d, S3a). This motion likely reflects intrinsic flexibility at the intron–tRNA junction, which contains a single-stranded region (Fig. 1d). These two states likely represent distinct local minima on the RNA’s energy landscape, reflecting dynamic sampling of catalytically permissive conformations prior to exon ligation.

Besides the tRNA exons, both the Pre-1S structures consist of the canonical RNA elements of group I intron (P2, P3, P4, P5, P6, P7, P8, P9, and P9.0) and adopts the canonical architecture seen in previously reported Azoarcus ribozyme structures16,29(Fig. S3b-c). This conservation underscores the structural stability of the catalytic domain even in the context of full-length tRNA exons and emphasizes the conservation of the group I intron fold. Together, our structures provide a high-resolution view of a full-length pre-tRNA substrate poised near the onset of catalysis, offering insight into early structural events associated with tRNA maturation and intron excision.

2-nt sliding of P1 helix between Linear Intron and Pre-tRNA
To investigate the structural transitions underpinning post-splicing and circularization of the Azoarcus group I intron, we determined high-resolution cryo-EM structures of the excised linear intron (L intron; Post-2S) and the subsequent circular introns (C and C′ introns; Post-C) at 3.01 Å resolution for L, 3.27 Å and 2.86 Å resolutions for C and C′ introns (Figs. 2-5, Figs. S4-6, Supplementary Table 1, and Supplementary Movie 1). These reconstructions allowed us to examine in detail how the intron architecture evolves following exon ligation and prepares for circularization.

Structural comparison between the Pre-1S and L intron states revealed that while the global scaffold of the ribozyme, including peripheral domains and the G-binding pocket, remained largely conserved, the P1/P1ext region underwent a notable conformational shift (Fig. 2b-e, Fig. S3d-e). In the Pre-1S state, the P1/P1ext helix is formed via base pairing between the 5′ exon and the internal guide sequence (IGS), aligning the 5′ splice site for nucleophilic attack. Following exon ligation and tRNA release, the P1ext helix is reformed within the intron alone, through intramolecular pairing between the free 5′ end and IGS. Importantly, the newly formed P1ext helix in the linear intron undergoes a 2-nt register shift relative to its position in the Pre-1S state, bringing the circularization reaction nucleophile, the 3′-OH of G205 (ωG, the 3′ terminal G) into planar alignment with the phosphodiester bond between U2 and U3, thus positioning the molecule in a circularization-ready conformation (Fig. 2f).

This finding highlights a key mechanism by which the ribozyme repurposes the same structural framework to carry out two distinct catalytic reactions: exon ligation and subsequent intron circularization. The observed register shift in the P1ext helix underscores the dynamic adaptability of group I introns, allowing them to reconfigure their base-pairing interactions to execute multiple reaction steps with high precision. In addition, we noticed that the density near the G-1 position in the L intron closely resembles the “pseudo-triple-helix” configuration recently described in another group I intron30. This region shows a continuous strand folding back onto the P1ext helix through non-canonical hydrogen bonds and stacking interactions, forming a pseudo-triple-helix–like tertiary contact (Fig. S4g). This interaction likely helps stabilize P1ext during circularization.

G37 reorientation anchors the circularization site and enhances efficiency
High-resolution cryo-EM structures of the L intron and the C intron revealed striking conservation across most of the ribozyme scaffold, particularly within the P1ext helix, which remains compact and nearly identical between the two states (Fig. 3a-b, Fig. S3f, S4, S5, S7, and Supplementary Movie 1). Despite this structural similarity, a single pronounced conformational change was observed during circularization: nucleotide G37 undergoes a distinct reorientation, flipping inward from its original outward-facing configuration while forming a Hoogsteen pair with G11 (Fig. 3c).

To assess the functional significance of G37, we performed site-directed mutagenesis to substitute this residue with A, C, or U, followed by in vitro circularization assays. Among the variants, the G37C mutant displayed a markedly increased yield of circular intron relative to the wild type (Fig. 3d), suggesting enhanced stabilization of the circularization site. This is likely due to the increased thermodynamic stability of the C37-G11 base pair compared to the original G-G pairing. In contrast, the G37A and G37U substitutions failed to promote circularization, indicating that the base-pairing potential and positioning of G37 are critical for productive catalysis. Together, these results identify G37 as a key conformational determinant in the circularization pathway of group I introns. Its dynamic reorientation not only marks a structural transition point but also fine-tunes the local architecture to optimize catalytic efficiency. This underscores a broader principle wherein single-nucleotide conformational switches can exert outsized influence on RNA processing outcomes by stabilizing transient but functionally important RNA configurations.

Identification and Validation of a Secondary Circularization Product
During prolonged incubation of Azoarcus pre-tRNA at 37°C, we observed the emergence of a lower-migrating RNA band beneath the canonical C intron, most clearly visible after 180 minutes (Fig. 1c). This unexpected product, designated as the C′ intron, suggested the possibility of an additional circular RNA species arising through a secondary processing event. The appearance of this smaller circular RNA recalls similar two-step circularization mechanisms reported in Tetrahymena group I introns31–34, prompting us to explore whether the Azoarcus system follows a comparable pathway. To investigate the origin of C′ intron, we conducted in vitro circularization assays using linear intron RNA. Gel electrophoresis revealed the presence of three distinct products: the C intron, the L-3 intron, and the C′ intron. This observation suggests that the C intron may undergo ring opening to form the L-3 linear intron33,34, which subsequently undergoes a second circularization event to generate the C′ intron, thereby supporting a model of sequential processing (Fig. 4a).

To validate the circular nature of both C and C′ introns, we treated the products with RNase R, a 3′-5′ exonuclease that selectively degrades linear RNAs while sparing circular forms. As expected, RNase R treatment led to complete degradation of the linear intron, while the C and C′ introns remained intact (Fig. 4b), confirming their circular topology35. We then employed reverse transcription followed by high-throughput sequencing to precisely map the ligation junctions of both products. Sequencing results revealed that the C intron is circularized at the L-3 position, resulting in the loss of the 5′-terminal GAU trinucleotide (Fig. 4c), whereas the C′ intron is circularized at the L-5 position, involving the removal of a GAUUU pentanucleotide (Fig. 4d). To test whether C′ intron formation occurs via a ring-opened intermediate, we purified C intron and incubated it under standard circularization conditions. Time-course experiments showed efficient conversion of C to C′ (Fig. 4e), confirming that C′ formation proceeds through secondary circularization following C intron opening33,34. Supporting this, 5′-FAM labeling detected only a 4-nt GGAU fragment corresponding to C intron formation, with no 6-nt GGAUUU fragment indicative of a direct conversion from L intron to C′ intron (Fig. 4f). Furthermore, inclusion of a recombinant RNase inhibitor to suppress potential enzymatic cleavage did not prevent the formation of the C′ intron (Fig. S8a). To further assess whether this conversion reflects a water driven, non-enzymatic process, we compared reactions performed under the original condition (pH 7.5) with those carried out under acidic conditions (pH 6.0). Under the neutral condition, hydrolysis of the C intron produced the linear L 3 intron and a clear C′ intron band was detected. In contrast, under acidic conditions, no detectable C′ intron was observed (Fig. S8b). Together, these observations support the interpretation that C′ intron formation is consistent with a water driven, non-enzymatic reaction that is intrinsic to the catalytic RNA.

To gain structural insight into the second circularization product, we determined the cryo-EM structure of the C′ intron at 2.86 Å resolution (Fig. 5a). The overall fold of the ribozyme remains largely conserved relative to the canonical C intron, however, pronounced structural remodeling occurs in the P1ext region (Fig. S3g). In contrast to the compact and fully base-paired P1ext observed in the C intron, the C′ intron displays extensive local unwinding, where nearly all base pairs in this region are disrupted except for the G11-G37 interaction, leaving the segment predominantly single-stranded (Fig. 5b-c and Fig. S7c). This partial melting appears to expand the solvent-exposed cavity adjacent to the catalytic center and may increase local flexibility near the ωG. The observed relaxation of P1ext is consistent with the biochemical evidence for a second, water-driven transesterification step, suggesting that such unwinding could facilitate repositioning of the phosphodiester bond between ωG and C5 for the subsequent ligation event. Together, these results reveal that the Azoarcus group I intron undergoes a two-step circularization process, highlighting a sequential and dynamic pathway reminiscent of Tetrahymena introns33,34.

Coordination of Catalytic Metal Ions Across Splicing and Circularization States
Metal ions play essential roles in group I intron catalysis, where five specific ions (M -M ) have been proposed to form the essential catalytic center. Through cryo-EM analysis of five functional states, including Pre-1S_a, Pre-1S_b, the L intron, the C intron, and the C′ intron, we identified and characterized three metal ion sites, designated M ,M and M (Fig. S9). The M ion displays state-dependent coordination geometry. In Pre-1S conformations, M associates with non-bridging phosphate oxygens of C87, G169, and A171 within the intron core. In the same states, M is positioned near the catalytic center and coordinates the nonbridging phosphate oxygens of G127 and A171, together with the 2′ and 3′ hydroxyl groups of ExoG. This coordination geometry suggests that M may contribute to stabilizing the leaving group and may act in concert with M to support a catalytically competent configuration. During the first circularization step, the key nucleotide U3 at the circularization site undergoes a conformational rearrangement that places its phosphate group within the coordination sphere of both M and M . This rearrangement likely anchors the circularization site within the catalytic core. Concurrently, M coordinates with the 2′ and 3′ hydroxyl groups of ωG, which may facilitate proper positioning of ωG during catalysis. The M ion lies peripherally to the active site and maintains stable coordination with the non-bridging phosphate oxygens of U172 and A173 in all observed states. This conserved geometry likely stabilizes the tertiary architecture of the P9.0 domain and contributes to maintaining the integrity of the ribozyme’s scaffold.

Beyond these established metal sites, we identified an additional ion in the catalytic core occupying the M position previously reported in Tetrahymena ribozymes14. This M coordinates the non-bridging phosphate oxygen of A86 and the 3′-OH of G127. The conservation of this position among group I introns suggests a possible catalytic or structural role, although its precise function remains to be determined. Together, these findings reveal that while the metallo-active core maintains a conserved overall architecture, the coordination geometries of individual ions adjust dynamically in response to transitions between splicing and circularization. This structural plasticity provides a mechanistic basis for how group I introns accommodate distinct chemical reactions while preserving catalytic precision.

Proposed Two-Step Circularization Mechanism
Integrating our structural and biochemical findings, along with previously established models such as the Tetrahymena IVS RNA circularization pathway31–34, we propose a two-step circularization mechanism for the Azoarcus pre-tRNA intron that operates through a “conformational rearrangement-sequential cleavage” framework (Fig. 5d). Following canonical self-splicing, the excised linear intron adopts a catalytically competent conformation through structural reorganization of the P1ext helix. This rearrangement aligns the phosphodiester bond between U2 and U3 within the ribozyme active site. The 3′-hydroxyl group of the conserved catalytic residue ωG then initiates a site-specific intramolecular transesterification reaction at U2, resulting in cleavage at the L-3 site and release of a 3-nt 5′ fragment (GAU). This first ligation event yields the primary circular species, termed the C intron. Subsequently, under near-neutral pH, the C intron undergoes spontaneous hydrolysis at the ligated junction, generating an L-3 linear intermediate33,34. This event promotes register shift of the P1ext helix, which in turn exposes a second phosphodiester bond between U4 and C5. A second transesterification reaction is then catalyzed by ωG, leading to cleavage at the L-5 site and release of a UU dinucleotide, ultimately forming the second circular product, C′ intron.

While this sequential pathway is supported by biochemical data, we cannot exclude the possibility of an alternative route. Specifically, a subset of linear introns may adopt a flexible P1ext conformation de novo, enabling ωG to bypass the L-3 reaction and directly cleave at the U4-C5 site32. This single-step mechanism would yield the C′ intron via release of a 5-nt fragment (GAUUU), reflecting a shortcut within the broader circularization pathway (Fig. 5d). However, as described above, our 5′-FAM labeling experiments detected no 6-nt GGAUUU product under standard in vitro conditions, confirming that direct conversion from the L intron to the C′ intron does not occur in our reconstituted system. While we cannot exclude the possibility that cellular factors or specific physiological conditions might enable this alternative route in vivo, our results indicate that the C intron-mediated sequential pathway represents the predominant mechanism of C′ intron formation under the tested conditions. Together, these results reveal a mechanistically versatile circularization program within group I introns, governed by dynamic P1ext remodeling and catalyzed through the strategic positioning of reactive residues and substrates. This work not only expands our understanding of intron self-processing but also provides a conceptual framework for engineering programmable RNA circularization systems.
